admonition.paragraph: This tutorial assumes that you have completed the earlier tutorials: Create and Launch a Basic Application with Hydra and Add a Command Line Interface to Our Application.

section.title: Design a Hierarchical Interface for an Application
section.paragraph: In this tutorial we will design an application that has an interface that is hierarchical in nature. This particular application will describe a player in a video game; this player has a configurable name and experience-level, as well as an inventory, which itself has configurable components.

section.title: Creating (Fake) Library Code
section.paragraph: Often times the interface of an application is determined by existing classes and functions in our library’s code. Let’s create a new Python script, game_library.py, in the same directory as my_app.py. This will serve as a mimic of a “real” Python library.
In this script we’ll define a Character class and an inventory() function as follows. Populate game_library.py with the following code.

container.caption: Contents of game_library.py

note.paragraph: Type-annotations are not required by hydra-zen. However, they do enable runtime type-checking of configured values for our application.

section.paragraph: To see this code in action, open a Python console (or Jupyter notebook) in the same directory as game_library.py and reproduce the following steps.

container.caption: Getting a feel for the code in game_library.py
container.literal_block:
>>> from game_library import Character, inventory >>> stuff = inventory(gold=12, weapon="stick", costume="bball jersey")
>>> Character("bowser", inventory=stuff) bowser, lvl: 1, has: {'gold': 12, 'weapon': 'stick', 'costume': 'bball jersey'}

section.title: Modifying Our Application
section.paragraph: Let’s change our application so that the interface describes only one player, instead of two. We want to be able to configure the player based on the following hierarchy of fields:
These fields reflect the interfaces/structure of Character and inventory().

section.title: Dynamically Generating Configs
section.paragraph: Because configurable aspects of our application should directly reflect the interfaces of Character class and inventory(), we can use builds() to generate configs that reflect these interfaces.
To see builds() in action, open a Python console (or Jupyter notebook) in the same directory as game_library.py. Follow along with these inputs.

container.caption: Getting a feel for builds()
container.literal_block:
>>> from hydra_zen import builds, instantiate, to_yaml >>> from game_library import Character
>>> def print_yaml(x): print(to_yaml(x))
>>> CharConf = builds(Character, populate_full_signature=True)
>>> print_yaml(CharConf) _target_: game_library.Character name: ??? level: 1 inventory: null
>>> print_yaml(CharConf(name="celeste")) _target_: game_library.Character name: celeste level: 1 inventory: null

section.paragraph: The instantiate() function is used to actually “build” the object described by our config

container.caption: Getting a feel for instantiate().
container.literal_block:
>>> from hydra_zen import instantiate
>>> char = instantiate(CharConf(name="celeste"))
>>> char celeste, lvl: 1, has: None
>>> isinstance(char, Character) True

section.paragraph: Let’s create a configuration for a character with basic “starter gear” for their inventory. We will use the following code in my_app.py.

container.caption: Dynamically generating configs based on game_library
container.literal_block:
from hydra_zen import make_custom_builds_fn
from game_library import inventory, Character
builds = make_custom_builds_fn(populate_full_signature=True)
InventoryConf = builds(inventory) starter_gear = InventoryConf(gold=10, weapon="stick", costume="tunic")
# note: # We are nesting the config for `inventory` within the # config for `Character`. CharConf = builds(Character, inventory=starter_gear)

section.title: Updating the Task Function
section.paragraph: We’ll make some modifications to our task function.

list_item.paragraph: We’re only dealing with one player now, not two, so we adjust accordingly.
Let’s print Character-instance for player so that we get instant feedback when we run our application from the CLI.

container.caption: A revised task function (single-player only)
container.literal_block:
def task_function(player: Character):
print(player)
with open("player_log.txt", "a") as f: f.write("Game session log:\n") f.write(f"Player: {player}\n")
return player

section.title: Piecing It All Together
section.paragraph: Combining these configs and task function together - along with the boilerplate code needed to create a command line interface - our updated my_app.py script is as follows.

container.caption: Contents of my_app.py:
container.literal_block:
from hydra_zen import make_custom_builds_fn, store, zen
from game_library import inventory, Character
builds = make_custom_builds_fn(populate_full_signature=True)
# generating configs starter_gear = builds(inventory, gold=10, weapon="stick", costume="tunic")
CharConf = builds(Character, inventory=starter_gear)
# Generate and store a top-level config specifying `CharConf` as the # default config for `player` @store(name="my_app", player=CharConf) def task_function(player: Character):
print(player)
with open("player_log.txt", "a") as f: f.write("Game session log:\n") f.write(f"Player: {player}\n")
return player
if __name__ == "__main__": store.add_to_hydra_store() zen(task_function).hydra_main(config_name="my_app", version_base="1.1", config_path=".", )

section.title: Running Our Application
section.paragraph: We can now configure any aspect of the player when launching our application; let’s try a few examples in order to get a feel for the syntax. Open your terminal in the directory shared by both my_app.py and game_library.py and run the following commands. Verify that you can reproduce the behavior shown below.

Checking the --help option of our application reveals the hierarchical structure of its configurable interface. See that the only required value is player.name, and that we can override any of the other default configured values.

container.caption: Checking the configurable components of our app. (We will add configuration groups in a later lesson.)
container.literal_block:
$ python my_app.py --help my_app is powered by Hydra.
== Configuration groups == Compose your configuration from those groups (group=option)
== Config == Override anything in the config (foo.bar=value)
player: _target_: game_library.Character name: ??? level: 1 inventory: _target_: game_library.inventory gold: 10 weapon: stick costume: tunic

section.paragraph: Now let’s run our application with various configurations.

container.caption: Configuring: name
container.literal_block: $ python my_app.py player.name=frodo frodo, lvl: 1, has: {'gold': 10, 'weapon': 'stick', 'costume': 'tunic'}

container.caption: Configuring: name and level
container.literal_block: $ python my_app.py player.name=frodo player.level=5 frodo, lvl: 5, has: {'gold': 10, 'weapon': 'stick', 'costume': 'tunic'}

container.caption: Configuring: name, level, and costume
container.literal_block: $ python my_app.py player.name=frodo player.level=2 player.inventory.costume=robe frodo, lvl: 2, has: {'gold': 10, 'weapon': 'stick', 'costume': 'robe'}

note.paragraph: We can use hydra_zen.launch() to launch our application, instead of using our application’s CLI. The following command line expression
note.literal_block: $ python my_app.py player.name=frodo player.level=2 player.inventory.costume=robe frodo, lvl: 2, has: {'gold': 10, 'weapon': 'stick', 'costume': 'robe'}
note.paragraph: can be replicated from a Python console via:

container.caption: A Python console, opened in the same directory as my_app.py
container.literal_block: >>> from hydra_zen import launch >>> from my_app import Config, task_function >>> job = launch( ... Config, ... task_function, ... ["player.name=frodo", "player.level=2", "player.inventory.costume=robe"], ... ) frodo, lvl: 2, has: {'gold': 10, 'weapon': 'stick', 'costume': 'robe'}

section.title: Inspecting the Results
section.paragraph: To inspect the most-recent log written by our application, let’s open a Python terminal in the same directory as my_app.py and define the following function for reading files
section.literal_block: >>> from pathlib import Path >>> def print_file(x: Path): ... with x.open("r") as f: ... print(f.read())
section.paragraph: Getting the directory containing the output of the most-recent job:
section.literal_block: >>> *_, latest_job = sorted((Path.cwd() / "outputs").glob("*/*")) >>> latest_job # changes based on reader's date, time, and OS WindowsPath('C:/outputs/2021-10-22/00-19-52')
section.paragraph: Let’s check the log file that our application wrote. player_log.txt should read as follows.
Hydra details the hierarchical config passed to our task function; let’s look at the contents of .hydra/config.yaml.
section.literal_block: >>> print_file(latest_job / ".hydra" / "config.yaml") player: _target_: game_library.Character name: frodo level: 2 inventory: _target_: game_library.inventory gold: 10 weapon: stick costume: robe
section.paragraph: We can also check to see what the exact “overrides” that were used to launch the application for this job in .hydra/overrides.yaml.

Great! Our application is now much more sophisticated: its configurable interface reflects - dynamically - the library code that we are ultimately instantiating. We also see the power of Hydra’s ability to configure nested fields within our config.
In the next tutorial, we will define swappable config groups so that we can load specific player profiles and inventory load-outs from our application’s interface.
